title: Heng O: Flight to the Moon
subtitle: An immortality pill in Werner's retelling

flight.author: E. T. C. Werner (modern compiler and author)
flight.translator: not applicable; authored in English by E. T. C. Werner
flight.locator: Chapter V · Myths of the Stars; Chapter V · Myths of the Stars, normalized characters 13857-14705
flight.excerpt: Heng O, during her husband's absence, saw a white light which seemed to issue from a beam in the roof, while a most delicious odour filled every room. By the aid of a ladder she reached up to the spot whence the light came, found the pill of immortality, and ate it. She suddenly felt that she was freed from the operation of the laws of gravity and as if she had wings, and was just essaying her first flight when Shen I returned. He went to look for his pill, and, not finding it, asked Heng O what had happened. The young wife, seized with fear, opened the window and flew out. Shen I took his bow and pursued her. The moon was full, the night clear, and he saw his wife flying rapidly in front of him, only about the size of a toad. Just when he was redoubling his pace to catch her up a blast of wind struck him to the ground like a dead leaf.
flight.note: Quotation from E. T. C. Werner's 1922 English synthesis; it is not a direct translation of the ancient source it discusses.

moon.author: E. T. C. Werner (modern compiler and author)
moon.translator: not applicable; authored in English by E. T. C. Werner
moon.locator: Chapter V · Myths of the Stars; Chapter V · Myths of the Stars, normalized characters 14706-15270
moon.excerpt: Heng O continued her flight until she reached a luminous sphere, shining like glass, of enormous size, and very cold. The only vegetation consisted of cinnamon-trees. No living being was to be seen. All of a sudden she began to cough, and vomited the covering of the pill of immortality, which was changed into a rabbit as white as the purest jade. This was the ancestor of the spirituality of the _yin_, or female, principle. Heng O noticed a bitter taste in her mouth, drank some dew, and, feeling hungry, ate some cinnamon. She took up her abode in this sphere.
moon.note: Quotation from E. T. C. Werner's 1922 English synthesis; it is not a direct translation of the ancient source it discusses.

narrativeBlocks.title: The pill is found
narrativeBlocks.body: In Werner's version, Heng O finds and eats a pill of immortality while Shen I is away. When he returns, she opens a window and flies out.

narrativeBlocks.title: A rabbit on a cold sphere
narrativeBlocks.body: Werner describes Heng O reaching a cold, luminous sphere. She coughs up the pill's covering, which changes into a white rabbit, and stays there.

narrativeBlocks.title: One version, not every telling
narrativeBlocks.body: The name here is Heng O, and the scene is Werner's early twentieth-century retelling. Do not treat its details as a universal or unchanging account of the moon story.

narrativeBlocks.title: The moon story has variants
narrativeBlocks.body: Werner's episode links immortality, flight, and the rabbit; other retellings can vary in names, motives, and details.
